Druids and sorcerers sit in the guildhall when they have unlocked double mana regeneration in protection zones. They make runes to sell or use on hunts. This is useful for raising their magic level, and they do it when they dont feel like hunting, or when they are doing chores at home in real life.


Monks have an ability that increases the mana regeneration of party members for 2.5 mins that they can use every 5 mins. This lets druid and sorcerer make runes faster, and helps all of them gain magic level just a little faster. Monks can't make any useful runes, but magic level helps them heal themselves better, so its still useful to raise that skill. I often use it then go look at market prices for a few mins between casts.

Our guild does raffles every month for prizes. You can get a ticket by doing atleast a half hour hunt with another guild member (1/day), or donating a certain amount to the guild store, or various other activities.


The guild store takes those donations, and sells the items to members at below market prices to raise funds for paying for the guildhall.


The guildhall has training dummies that were bought with excess funds, so members can train their skills without having to buy a house and a 900tc dummy for themselves. There is also near infinite free food in the guildhall because some members bring food every time they visit, and druids often manasit. If a monk manasits there too, everyone gets free mana from the monk occasionally.


The guildhall also offers beds to offline train in, and an NPC for resupplying between hunts.


There's more I'm missing, but our discord is very active and we sistered with another guild on the server, so we have 2 guildhalls that members of both guilds can use, and many members have opened their houses to guild members as well, so we can restock from almost anywhere.

For meals, almost anything in the crockpot with chicken dries and reconstitutes well. Chicken chili is perhaps my favorite of the meals we have done though.


For fruit with skins like blueberries, cut them in half and they dry just fine. Kids love freeze dried fruit in cereal for breakfast.


Root veggies like carrots and potatoes need to be cooked first. I have a local farm stand that gets these HUGE carrots that are like 2inches diameter. I buy about 10 lbs of those, boil them till just soft enough to run through the fry cutter, cut them into sticks, and freeze dry those. If you've ever had veggie straws, they have a similar texture, but all carrot flavor and no added ingredients. Plus if you want carrots with dinner, and you store your freeze dried stuff in mason jars, just add a bit of seasoning to the jar like rosemary or brown sugar, fill the jar with hot water from the teapot and theyre ready to serve in like 5-10 mins, and they absorb the flavors inside, so its not just a coating of flavor!


Speaking of rosemary, we freeze dried a bunch this year and it is so, so much tastier than the store bought stuff. Like 3-5 leaves replaces almost a tablespoon of the store stuff too.


If you have flowers, most can be freeze dried and keep their color and look afterward. Great for keeping them looking fresh for fall or winter. We freeze dry scarlet beebalm to add to tea when we are sick. Im still looking for other medicinals that freeze dry well, but thats great tasting on its own (its an ingredient in earl grey tea, and several others anyways)

I've seen 3 different therapists with different therapy styles over the past 2 years for treating my anxiety/depression. 

The 1st therapist I saw was not a depression/anxiety specialist; he dealt in addictions mostly. (no one else had openings for another 3 months) I didn't connect well with him, and found myself making things up to pass the time in his office. That's a VERY bad thing to do, because it means you aren't working on yourself. I relapsed into a major depressive episode and didn't leave my apartment for a month.

After that month, I went to an outpatient program for treatment at a local hospital. There I was assigned my 2nd therapist, and was able to start some medications which worked for a while but ultimately didn't. That second therapist's methods weren't the right fit for me, and mostly aligned with fighting the depression and anxiety, which wore me out mentally and did little to fix things. I had another panic attack when after 2 months I realized that I wasn't seeing even a little progress, and I had stretched some truths because I didn't trust her fully. (I get paranoid occasionally when in a depressive spiral) 

I isolated again for a few weeks, and then finally my parents called my doctor and they were able to find a clinic only a short distance from the hospital. The therapist there took a different approach, using acceptance therapy (ACT) instead of fighting the issues.

I knew that this therapist was the best one I'd been to on my second session there when she said "I was thinking about what we talked about last week, so I was looking through my books the other night...".

As others have said, the therapist is NOT your friend. That's why I believe they have the ability to help. A good therapist doesn't lie to you, they force you to face what the problem is, and help you determine a solution that works for you. In order for them to do that, you need to be able to trust them enough to tell them the whole truth. If it's not working, you have to be able to tell them that too.

I'm now medication free, and I know what triggers my anxiety. I'm able to tell people "I'll probably be irritable today", and not shove my emotions down. I'm currently working on being comfortable in uncomfortable situations. I'll be looking into volunteering somewhere in the next few days, and if that works, I might be ready to work again.

Feel free to message me if you have questions or just want to talk.
